messages.content: ## How commercial machine translation engines protect entities and numbers: Google Cloud Translation glossaries and do-not-translate, DeepL glossaries, ModernMT adaptive MT, Microsoft Translator custom glossaries — features and documented behavior I'll research each engine's entity/number protection features systematically. Let me start with parallel searches on the main topics. --- ## Academic NMT research on named entity and number preservation: copy mechanisms, pointer-generator networks, entity annotation/replacement methods (e.g., Umugwaneza et al., Bunk et al.), and documented NMT failure modes for numbers, names, and inline markup # NMT Research on Named Entity & Number Preservation — Summary of Findings ## 1. Background: the rare-word problem Early NMT with fixed vocabularies mapped rare tokens — proper names, numbers, markup — to ``, causing omissions and artifacts. Luong et al. (2015) documented this systematically, categorized rare-word errors (names, numbers, etc.), and showed post-hoc fixes (alignment-based UNK replacement, a copy mechanism, and a "positional all-transduce" method targeting numbers) recover up to ≈+2.8 BLEU on WMT'14 [1]. Koehn & Knowles (2017) listed rare words as one of six persistent NMT challenges, showing sharp quality degradation as rare-word density rises [17]. BPE subword models (Sennrich et al., 2016) largely solved open-vocabulary translation [3], but did not fully fix numbers (arbitrary digit grouping) or entity-level phenomena (transliteration choice, cross-sentence consistency). ## 2. Copy mechanisms and pointer-generator networks - **CopyNet** (Gu et al., 2016): end-to-end copying via "predictive copying," able to copy token segments; improves handling of rare tokens and names [4]. - **Pointer-softmax** (Gulcehre et al., 2016): hybrid generate/copy switch for NMT; gains concentrated on named entities and diminished in large-data/large-vocabulary regimes (where BPE already covers most tokens) [5]. - **Pointer-sentinel** (Merity et al., 2016/17): pointer mechanism for language modeling; canonical reference in the pointer-model lineage [6]. - **Pointer-generator** (See et al., 2017): mixes the generation softmax with an attention-derived copy distribution (plus coverage); despite being a summarization paper, this is the standard "pointer-generator network" architecture adopted by later NMT work [7]. - **Low-resource evidence**: Umugwaneza et al. (AFRICON 2023) compared an LSTM attention seq2seq baseline, CopyNet, and a pointer-generator for Kinyarwanda→English; copy-augmented models outperformed the baseline, with error analysis showing better retention of named entities, numbers, and OOV words [8]. - Known limitation: the copy/generate decision can miscalibrate — over-copying words that should be translated, or failing to copy when needed [4][5][7]. ## 3. Entity annotation / replacement methods - **Source-side annotation**: appending NER tags (with lemma/POS) as input features improved entity translation [9]. - **Placeholder masking/replacement**: detect entities with NER, replace them with type-tagged unique placeholders in training and inference, then re-insert translations. Bunk et al. (2019) applied this for English→German, reporting BLEU gains and fewer entity errors (with dictionary-based re-substitution and copy fallback) [10]. Hoang et al. (2018) used entity masking with unique identifiers during back-translation to force the model to copy entities [11]. - **Lexicons and hard constraints**: soft lexicon biasing improves rare-word/entity output [12]; lexically constrained decoding enforces required target terms [13][14]; Dinu et al. (2019) trained models to apply glossaries via placeholder-style special tokens, improving exact term usage [15]. - **Retrieval**: kNN-MT retrieves similar (source, target) pairs from a translation memory, helping rare-token and entity consistency [16]. - **Character-level modeling**: fully character-level NMT handles names without segmentation artifacts [21]. ## 4. Documented failure modes **Numbers** - Pre-BPE: numbers frequently became UNKs [1]. With subwords: digit strings are split into arbitrary fragments → dropped, duplicated, or mistranslated digits; poor generalization to unseen lengths/values; verbatim source-copying even when locale conventions differ (decimal/grouping separators, dates) [3][17][18][20]. - Language-model studies confirm digit sequences are poorly modeled without format-aware treatment [18]. - Mitigations: digit-aware/protected tokenization, copy mechanisms, placeholder protection, constrained decoding, numeric post-validation [1][4][10][13][14][15]. **Names** - Rare/unseen person and place names → UNK omission, hallucination, inconsistent transliteration, or copying when an established target-language exonym exists; strong sensitivity to character-level noise (typos, casing) [1][17][19]. - Entity errors are among the highest-severity categories in MQM-style quality evaluation [20]. - Mitigations: copy/pointer models (especially low-resource) [4][5][8]; entity masking/replacement [10][11]; lexicons/constraints [12][13][14][15]; retrieval [16]. **Inline markup (tags, placeholders)** - Models trained on plain text delete, duplicate, misorder, or misnest tags and corrupt placeholders (`%s`, `{0}`, ``); long-range reordering makes positional preservation hard. These surface as "design/markup" and "locale convention" errors in MQM-based QA [20]; localization-industry reports consistently flag tag/placeholder corruption as a top NMT failure mode. - Mitigations in the literature: treat tags/placeholders as atomic protected tokens via masking [10][11]; enforce presence via lexical constraints during decoding [13][14][15]; validate output post hoc. ## 5. Synthesis The literature converges on a layered recipe: (1) subword tokenization as the baseline [3]; (2) copy/pointer mechanisms for low-resource settings where entities and numbers dominate the OOV mass [4][5][7][8]; (3) NER-driven placeholder masking with re-insertion for production/localization pipelines [10][11]; (4) hard terminology constraints or retrieval when specific terms must be preserved [13][14][15][16]; and (5) numeric/format validation, since no architectural fix fully eliminates digit and markup errors [18][20]. ## References [1] Luong, Pham & Manning (2015). *Addressing the Rare Word Problem in Neural Machine Translation.* ACL. [2] Jean et al. (2015). *On Using Very Large Target Vocabulary for Neural Machine Translation.* ACL. [3] Sennrich, Haddow & Birch (2016). *Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units.* ACL. [4] Gu, Lu, Li & Li (2016). *Incorporating Copying Mechanism in Sequence-to-Sequence Learning.* ACL. [5] Gulcehre et al. (2016). *Pointing the Way to Effective Translation.* ACL. [6] Merity, Xiong, Bradbury & Socher (2016/17). *Pointer Sentinel Mixture Models.* ICLR 2017. [7] See, Liu & Manning (2017). *Get To The Point: Summarization with Pointer-Generator Networks.* ACL. [8] Umugwaneza, Niyomwungeri & Nshimiyimana (2023). *Enhancing Kinyarwanda–English Neural Machine Translation with Copy Mechanisms.* IEEE AFRICON. [9] Sennrich & Haddow (2016). *Linguistic Input Features Improve Neural Machine Translation.* ACL. [10] Bunk, Halbach, Hämmerl & Vu (2019). *Improving Neural Machine Translation for German with Named Entity Handling.* [11] Hoang, Koehn, Haffari & Cohn (2018). *Iterative Back-Translation for Neural Machine Translation.* WNMT@ACL. [12] Arthur, Neubig & Nakamura (2016). *Incorporating Discrete Translation Lexicons into Neural Machine Translation.* EMNLP. [13] Hokamp & Liu (2017). *Traversing Oceans of Text: Terminology Constraints in Neural Machine Translation.* ACL (short). [14] Post & Vilar (2018). *Fast Lexically Constrained Decoding with Dynamic Beam Allocation for NMT.* NAACL. [15] Dinu, Mathur, Federico & Al-Onaizan (2019). *Training Neural Machine Translation to Apply Terminology Constraints.* ACL. [16] Khandelwal, Fan, Jurafsky, Zettlemoyer & Lewis (2021). *Nearest Neighbor Machine Translation.* ICLR. [17] Koehn & Knowles (2017). *Six Challenges for Neural Machine Translation.* WNMT@ACL. [18] Spithourakis & Riedel (2018). *Numeracy for Language Models: Evaluating and Improving Their Ability to Predict Numbers.* ACL. [19] Belinkov & Bisk (2018). *Synthetic and Natural Noise Both Break Neural Machine Translation.* ICLR. [20] Lommel, Uszkoreit & Burchardt (2014). *Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM): A Framework for Declaring and Describing Translation Quality Metrics.* Tradumàtica. [21] Lee, Cho & Hofmann (2017). *Fully Character-Level Neural Machine Translation without Explicit Segmentation.* TACL. *Caveat: citation details (venues/years for [8] and [10] in particular) are reconstructed from memory and should be verified against ACL Anthology/IEEE Xplore before formal use.* --- ## Translator and editor practical checklist for preserving entities, numbers, and markup in localized output: DNT handling, tag integrity, number verification, and locale-adapted formatting rules # Localized Output QA Checklist: DNT, Tags, Numbers, Locale Formatting Consolidated from established localization standards and platform style guides [1][2][3][4]. --- ## 1. DNT (Do-Not-Translate) Handling - [ ] **Identify DNT classes before starting**: brand/product names, trademarks, code identifiers, variable/function names, file paths, URLs, email addresses, commands, API keys, version/model numbers, legal entity names. - [ ] **Load the project glossary with DNT terms flagged** in your CAT tool (terminology recognition / locked terms); do not rely on memory alone. - [ ] **Copy DNT strings exactly**: preserve casing, spacing, hyphenation, and punctuation. No transliteration unless the glossary specifies a localized brand form for that market. - [ ] **Watch for false DNT look-alikes** — common nouns that resemble product names (e.g., "Finder," "Edge," "Swift"). - [ ] **Protect placeholders/variables** in all syntaxes: `{0}`, `%s`, `%1$s`, `%@`, `{{name}}`, `${var}`, `%d`. Never translate, reorder, or delete them; reposition them only as target grammar requires. - [ ] **Run a pseudo-localization pass** pre- and post-translation to surface leaked DNT strings (untranslated source text appearing in the build, or translated text where DNT was required) [2]. ## 2. Tag / Markup Integrity - [ ] **Preserve all inline tags**; run the CAT tool's tag-validation check before delivery. Tag count and pairing must match source even when tag *position* shifts for target word order. - [ ] **Never break nesting order** of paired tags (`……` must close in reverse order); orphan/unpaired tags are the #1 cause of build failures. - [ ] **HTML/XML**: translate only translatable attribute values (`alt`, `title`, `aria-label`, `placeholder`); never touch element names, attribute names, `id`/`class`, `href` (unless a locale-specific URL is specified), or `
